Scoring Rules and Forecast Evaluation

Source: vignettes/scoring-and-evaluation.Rmd
scoring-and-evaluation.Rmd

Overview

Rigorous forecast evaluation requires proper scoring rules — metrics that are optimised when the forecaster reports their true belief. mortensor implements a comprehensive set of scoring functions for both point forecasts and probabilistic forecasts.

This vignette covers:

  1. The accuracy() method: one-call evaluation from a mort_forecast object
  2. The compare_accuracy() function: tabular comparison across models
  3. Point forecast metrics: RMSE, MAE, MASE (cell, trend, combined)
  4. Probabilistic metrics: CRPS (Gaussian and empirical), interval score, WIS, log-score
  5. How these are used in model selection and calibration
  6. Practical examples for comparing models

The accuracy() method

The simplest way to evaluate a forecast is to call accuracy() directly on a mort_forecast object. It computes all relevant metrics in one call.

Out-of-sample evaluation

When you have held-out observed data, pass it as the test argument:

library(mortensor)
data(example_mortality)

# Split data: first 80% for training, last 20% for testing
n_t    <- example_mortality$n_t
n_test <- round(0.2 * n_t)
train  <- example_mortality[, 1:(n_t - n_test), ]
test   <- example_mortality[, (n_t - n_test + 1):n_t, ]

# Build forecast from training data
sm  <- smooth_mortality(train, method = "gam", covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))
cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE)
fc  <- forecast(cal, h = n_test)
fc  <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

# One call — all metrics
acc <- accuracy(fc, test = test)
print(acc)
# <mort_accuracy>  out_of_sample
#   Model:           Ensemble
#   Evaluated on:    13 ages x 4 years x 10 groups
#   --- Point forecast ---
#   MASE (combined): 0.8234
#   MASE (cell):     0.8567
#   MASE (trend):    0.7456
#   RMSE (log):      0.0312
#   MAE:             1.23e-03
#   --- Probabilistic ---
#   Coverage (95%):  0.943
#   Interval score:  0.1287
#   CRPS:            0.0198

The result is a mort_accuracy object. All fields are accessible:

acc$mase_combined   # 0.8234
acc$coverage        # 0.943
acc$crps            # 0.0198

In-sample evaluation

Without test data, accuracy() evaluates fitted values against the raw training data:

acc_in <- accuracy(fc)
print(acc_in)
# <mort_accuracy>  in_sample

Comparing multiple models with compare_accuracy()

To compare several models side-by-side, use compare_accuracy():

# Calibrate individual models
cal_coda <- calibrate(sm, models = "tucker3_coda", ensemble = FALSE)
cal_lc   <- calibrate(sm, models = "lee_carter",   ensemble = FALSE)
cal_ets  <- calibrate(sm, models = "ets",           ensemble = FALSE)
cal_ens  <- calibrate(sm, ensemble = TRUE)

# Forecast each
fc_coda <- add_pi(forecast(cal_coda, h = n_test), n_sim = 500)
fc_lc   <- add_pi(forecast(cal_lc,   h = n_test), n_sim = 500)
fc_ets  <- add_pi(forecast(cal_ets,  h = n_test), n_sim = 500)
fc_ens  <- add_pi(forecast(cal_ens,  h = n_test), n_sim = 500)

# Compare — returns a data.table sorted by MASE
comp <- compare_accuracy(
  "Tucker3-CoDa" = fc_coda,
  "Lee-Carter"   = fc_lc,
  "ETS"          = fc_ets,
  "Ensemble"     = fc_ens,
  test = test
)
print(comp)
#            model  mase_combined  mase_cell  mase_trend  rmse_log  ...
# 1:       Ensemble        0.809      0.847       0.721    0.028
# 2:  Tucker3-CoDa        0.823      0.857       0.745    0.031
# 3:    Lee-Carter        0.890      0.923       0.812    0.035
# 4:           ETS        0.991      1.034       0.923    0.042

You can also pass pre-computed mort_accuracy objects if you want to avoid re-computing:

acc1 <- accuracy(fc_coda, test = test)
acc2 <- accuracy(fc_lc,   test = test)
comp <- compare_accuracy("Tucker3-CoDa" = acc1, "Lee-Carter" = acc2)

Point forecast metrics

RMSE on log scale

Root mean squared error on log(mx)\log(m_x):

RMSElog=1n∑i(log(m̂i)−log(mi))2\text{RMSE}_{\log} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i} \bigl(\log(\hat{m}_i) - \log(m_i)\bigr)^2}

library(mortensor)

# Vectors of actual and predicted rates
rmse <- compute_rmse_log(actual = obs_mx, predicted = fc_mx)
cat("RMSE (log):", round(rmse, 4), "\n")

Mean absolute error

MAE=1n∑i|mi−m̂i|\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i |m_i - \hat{m}_i|

mae <- compute_mae(actual = obs_mx, predicted = fc_mx)

MASE: Mean Absolute Scaled Error

MASE is the primary metric used for model selection in mortensor. It normalises the MAE by the in-sample naive (random walk) forecast error:

MASE=MAEforecastMAEnaive\text{MASE} = \frac{\text{MAE}_{\text{forecast}}}{\text{MAE}_{\text{naive}}}

where MAEnaive=1T−1∑t=2T|yt−yt−1|\text{MAE}_{\text{naive}} = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=2}^T |y_t - y_{t-1}| on the training data.

A MASE < 1 means the model beats the naive random walk; MASE > 1 means it does worse.

Single series 

mase_val <- compute_mase(
  actual_test    = test_series,       # test period values
  predicted_test = forecast_series,   # forecast values
  train_series   = train_series       # training period values
)
cat("MASE:", round(mase_val, 3), "\n")

Cell-level MASE (across the full array)

Computes MASE for each (age, group) cell and averages:

mase_cell <- compute_mase_array(
  arr_test  = mx_test,     # 3D test array [n_ages x n_test x n_groups]
  fc_arr    = mx_forecast, # 3D forecast array [n_ages x h x n_groups]
  arr_train = mx_train     # 3D training array
)
cat("Cell MASE:", round(mase_cell, 3), "\n")

Group-trend MASE

Averages across ages first (collapsing to group-level trends), then computes MASE on these smoother series:

mase_trend <- compute_mase_group_trend(
  arr_test  = mx_test,
  fc_arr    = mx_forecast,
  arr_train = mx_train
)
cat("Trend MASE:", round(mase_trend, 3), "\n")

Combined MASE (used for model selection)

The combined MASE balances cell-level accuracy with trend accuracy:

MASEcombined=0.7×MASEcell+0.3×MASEtrend\text{MASE}_{\text{combined}} = 0.7 \times \text{MASE}_{\text{cell}} + 0.3 \times \text{MASE}_{\text{trend}}

mase_comb <- compute_mase_combined(
  arr_test  = mx_test,
  fc_arr    = mx_forecast,
  arr_train = mx_train
)
cat("Combined MASE:", round(mase_comb, 3), "\n")

Why 0.7/0.3? Cell-level accuracy is weighted more because it captures age-specific patterns, but trend accuracy prevents selecting models that are accurate on average while missing overall mortality decline trajectories.

Probabilistic forecast metrics

CRPS: Continuous Ranked Probability Score

The CRPS evaluates the full predictive distribution. Lower is better.

Gaussian CRPS (closed-form)

If the predictive distribution is 𝒩(μ,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2):

CRPS(F,y)=σ[y−μσ(2Φ(y−μσ)−1)+2ϕ(y−μσ)−1π]\text{CRPS}(F, y) = \sigma \left[ \frac{y - \mu}{\sigma}\left(2\Phi\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right) - 1\right) + 2\phi\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \right]

crps_g <- compute_crps_gaussian(
  obs   = log_obs,    # log(mx) observations
  mu    = log_mu,     # predictive means (log scale)
  sigma = log_sigma   # predictive standard deviations (log scale)
)
cat("Gaussian CRPS:", round(crps_g, 4), "\n")

Empirical CRPS (from bootstrap samples)

When the predictive distribution is represented by bootstrap samples:

CRPS(F,y)=1B∑b=1B|y−x(b)|−12B2∑b=1B∑b′=1B|x(b)−x(b′)|\text{CRPS}(F, y) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}|y - x^{(b)}| - \frac{1}{2B^2}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{b'=1}^{B}|x^{(b)} - x^{(b')}|

crps_e <- compute_crps_empirical(
  obs_arr  = mx_test,     # 3D observed array
  sims_arr = fc$sims      # 4D simulation array [n_a x h x n_g x n_sim]
)
cat("Empirical CRPS:", round(crps_e, 4), "\n")

The empirical CRPS is computed on the log scale for numerical stability.

Interval Score

The interval score evaluates a (1−α)(1-\alpha)-level prediction interval:

ISα(l,u;y)=(u−l)+2α(l−y)𝟏(y<l)+2α(y−u)𝟏(y>u)\text{IS}_\alpha(l, u; y) = (u - l) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(l - y)\mathbf{1}(y < l) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y - u)\mathbf{1}(y > u)

It rewards narrow intervals but heavily penalises observations falling outside.

Single observation 

is_val <- compute_interval_score(
  obs   = log_obs,     # scalar or vector
  lower = log_lower,   # lower PI bound (log scale)
  upper = log_upper,   # upper PI bound (log scale)
  alpha = 0.05         # for 95% PI
)
cat("Interval score:", round(is_val, 4), "\n")

Full 3D array 

is_arr <- compute_interval_score_array(
  obs_arr   = mx_test,       # 3D observed array
  lower_arr = fc$mx_lower,   # 3D lower bound
  upper_arr = fc$mx_upper,   # 3D upper bound
  alpha     = 0.05
)
cat("Mean interval score:", round(is_arr, 4), "\n")

The array version operates on log(mx)\log(m_x) internally.

Weighted Interval Score (WIS)

WIS generalises the interval score to multiple quantile levels, providing a single summary of the full predictive distribution:

WIS=1K+0.5[12|y−ŷ0.5|+∑k=1Kαk⋅ISαk]\text{WIS} = \frac{1}{K+0.5}\left[\frac{1}{2}|y - \hat{y}_{0.5}| + \sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_k \cdot \text{IS}_{\alpha_k}\right]

# quantile_matrix: [n_obs x K] matrix of quantile forecasts
# probs: K probabilities (e.g. c(0.025, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.975))

wis <- compute_wis(
  obs             = obs_vector,
  quantile_matrix = qmat,
  probs           = c(0.025, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.975)
)
cat("WIS:", round(wis, 4), "\n")

WIS is particularly useful for comparing models that produce different numbers of quantiles or when you want a single number summarising the entire predictive distribution.

Log-score (negative)

The log-score measures the probability density assigned to the observation:

LS(F,y)=−logf(y)\text{LS}(F, y) = -\log f(y)

where ff is the predictive density. Lower is better.

ls <- compute_log_score_gaussian(
  obs   = log_obs,
  mu    = log_mu,
  sigma = log_sigma
)
cat("Negative log-score:", round(ls, 4), "\n")

How metrics are used in model selection

Inside calibrate()

The calibrate() function uses combined MASE for:

  1. Tucker3 rank selection: The rank combination with lowest CV MASE is chosen
  2. Model comparison: All models are ranked by holdout combined MASE
  3. Ensemble weighting: Inverse-MASE weights: wi∝1/MASEiw_i \propto 1/\text{MASE}_i

Inside compare_models()

The comparison data.table contains three MASE variants:

sm  <- smooth_mortality(example_mortality, method = "gam",
                        covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))
cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE)

print(cal$comparison)
#              model   mase  mase_trend  mase_combined
# 1:    Tucker3-CoDa  0.847      0.721         0.809
# 2:  Tucker3-Direct  0.891      0.756         0.851
# 3:      Lee-Carter  0.923      0.812         0.890
# ...

Practical evaluation workflow

Using accuracy() (recommended)

The accuracy() method handles all the array extraction and alignment automatically:

data(example_mortality)

# Split into train and test mort_data objects
n_t    <- example_mortality$n_t
n_test <- round(0.2 * n_t)
train  <- example_mortality[, 1:(n_t - n_test), ]
test   <- example_mortality[, (n_t - n_test + 1):n_t, ]

# Pipeline on training data
sm  <- smooth_mortality(train, method = "gam", covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))
cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE)
fc  <- forecast(cal, h = n_test)
fc  <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

# All metrics in one call
acc <- accuracy(fc, test = test)
print(acc)

Comparing multiple models with compare_accuracy() 

# Calibrate individual models on the same training data
models <- c("tucker3_coda", "tucker3_direct", "lee_carter", "ets", "rwd")
forecasts <- list()
for (m in models) {
  cal_m <- calibrate(sm, models = m, ensemble = FALSE)
  fc_m  <- forecast(cal_m, h = n_test)
  fc_m  <- add_pi(fc_m, n_sim = 500)
  forecasts[[m]] <- fc_m
}

# One-line comparison table (sorted by MASE)
comp <- compare_accuracy(
  "Tucker3-CoDa"   = forecasts$tucker3_coda,
  "Tucker3-Direct"  = forecasts$tucker3_direct,
  "Lee-Carter"      = forecasts$lee_carter,
  "ETS"             = forecasts$ets,
  "RWD"             = forecasts$rwd,
  test = test
)
print(comp)

Low-level evaluation (manual array extraction)

The low-level compute_*() functions remain available for custom workflows:

# Manual train/test split at the array level
mx_train <- sm$mx
mx_test  <- test$mx

fc_arr <- tucker3_coda_forecast(
  mx_array = mx_train,
  years    = sm$years,
  ages     = sm$ages,
  h        = n_test,
  R_A = 3, R_B = 2, R_C = 2,
  ts_method = "ets"
)$mx_forecast

# Individual metrics
cat("MASE (cell):", round(compute_mase_array(mx_test, fc_arr, mx_train), 3), "\n")
cat("MASE (trend):", round(compute_mase_group_trend(mx_test, fc_arr, mx_train), 3), "\n")
cat("MASE (combined):", round(compute_mase_combined(mx_test, fc_arr, mx_train), 3), "\n")
cat("RMSE (log):", round(compute_rmse_log(mx_test, fc_arr), 4), "\n")

Metric selection guide

Metric Type Evaluates When to use
accuracy() All All metrics at once Default for mort_forecast objects
compare_accuracy() All Multi-model table Comparing several forecasts
compute_mase_combined() Point Overall forecast quality Low-level / custom workflows
compute_mase_array() Point Cell-level patterns Age-group accuracy matters
compute_mase_group_trend() Point Trend capture Decline trajectory matters
compute_rmse_log() Point Log-scale fit Traditional comparison
compute_crps_empirical() Prob. Full distribution Bootstrap-based forecasts
compute_crps_gaussian() Prob. Full distribution Gaussian assumption valid
compute_interval_score() Prob. Interval calibration Evaluating 95% PIs
compute_wis() Prob. Multi-quantile summary Comparing distributional forecasts
compute_log_score_gaussian() Prob. Density quality Gaussian density evaluation

Recommendations

  • Quick evaluation: accuracy(fc, test = holdout) — one call, all metrics
  • Multi-model comparison: compare_accuracy(..., test = holdout) — sorted table
  • Model selection: Combined MASE (used automatically by calibrate())
  • PI evaluation: Check coverage (should be near 0.95) + interval_score
  • Publication: Report MASE (point) + CRPS (distributional) + interval score (interpretable)
  • Multi-model papers: Use WIS with matched quantile levels across models

Summary

  • accuracy() computes all metrics from a mort_forecast object in one call
  • compare_accuracy() produces a tidy comparison table across models
  • Combined MASE (0.7 cell + 0.3 trend) is the workhorse for automated model selection
  • Probabilistic scores (CRPS, IS, WIS) evaluate the full predictive distribution and PI calibration
  • Low-level compute_*() functions remain available for custom workflows
  • The calibrate() pipeline integrates these scores seamlessly into the model selection workflow
